sections.heading: 1. General experimental
sections.preamble: All reactions were performed in a dry reaction vessel under a positive nitrogen atmosphere. Air- and moisture-sensitive compounds were transferred using syringes or spatulas under a nitrogen atmosphere. Analytical TLC was performed using TLC Silica gel 60 F254 plates (Merck,1.05554.0007), with visualization achieved by exposure to UV light at 254 nm, followed by treatment in an iodine chamber. The crude product was passed through a short column using ethyl acetate to extract the organic components, which were then concentrated under reduced pressure using a rotary evaporator (BUCHI Rotavapor R-100). Final purification was carried out by column chromatography on 60-120 mesh silica gel (Spectrochem) with an EtOAc/hexane mixture in the desired ratio.

records.text:
NMR spectroscopy
The 1H NMR (400 MHz) and 13C NMR (100 MHz) spectra were recorded on a Bruker Avance-400 spectrometer. The proton chemical shift values are expressed in parts per million (ppm, δ scale) downfield from tetramethylsilane (TMS) and are referenced to TMS (δ 0.0) and CHCl3 (δ 7.26). The chemical shifts for carbon are presented in parts per million (ppm, δ scale) downfield from TMS and referenced to the carbon resonance of CDCl3 (δ 77.16). The NMR data are reported as chemical shift, multiplicity (s = singlet, d = doublet, t = triplet, q = quartet, quint = quintet, sext = sextet, sept = septet, m = multiplet or multiple resonances, br = broad), coupling constant in hertz (Hz), and signal area integration in natural numbers.
IR analysis The IR spectra were recorded using an Agilent Cary 630 FTIR spectrometer, and the characteristic absorption bands are reported in cm⁻¹.
HRMS
High-resolution mass spectra (HRMS) were obtained using fast atom bombardment (FAB) ionization on a Q-TOF mass spectrometer (serial no. YA 263).

sections.heading: 3. Optimization of reaction conditions:
sections.preamble: In order to establish standardized reaction conditions, numerous experiments were conducted by varying parameters such as solvent, base, catalyst, and temperature, using the representative reaction between benzenesulfonamide and chlorobenzene. The experimental findings are summarized in Table 1. When various organic solvents were employed in combination with the Fe(acac)₃/CuI catalyst system and potassium carbonate as a base, at 130 °C for 24 hours under argon atmosphere on an oil bath, the desired N-phenylbenzenesulfonamide product 1 was obtained from 30% to 79% yield (entries 1–3). However, the desired product was not formed when toluene was used as the solvent (entry 2). The reaction was additionally conducted in the absence of solvent (neat) conditions, affording product 1 in 76% yield (entry 4). This yield is comparable to that achieved with DMSO as the solvent (entry 1). In light of this observation, the reaction was conducted using a reduced volume of DMSO (100 µL for a 0.5 mmol scale), resulting in an improved yield of 84% (entry 5). Using this reaction condition, sodium carbonate as the base was also examined, but it failed to enhance the product’s yield (entry 6). When base like KOH was employed, no desired product was obtained (entry 7). Variations of Fe(III) catalysts, including FeF₃ and FeCl₃, were investigated, but both failed to deliver satisfactory product formation (entries 8 and 9). The reaction carried out with Fe(acac)₂ afforded the desired product in 53% yield (entry 10), which is satisfactory but lower than the yield obtained using Fe(acac)₃ (entry 5). As part of the optimization, the reaction was carried out by sequentially omitting CuI, Fe(acac)₃, and then both catalysts. Under each of these conditions, only trace amounts or no desired product were observed (entries 11–13). This observation indicates that both catalysts play an essential role in the reaction system. During optimization (entries 14 and 15), we examined the effect of conducting the reaction under either an inert atmosphere or open air. The nitrogen atmosphere afforded higher yields compared to both argon and open air conditions. Lower reaction temperatures showed no enhancement in yield or conversion (entry 16). The catalyst loading was optimized to 5 mol% for each catalyst, 3 resulting in an 88% yield of the product (entry 17). Reducing the reaction time to 15 hours resulted in the highest yield of product 1, reaching 92% (entry 18). Decreasing the reaction time beyond 15 hours resulted in lower product yields (entry 19).

sections.heading: 6. Experimental procedure for catalyst recovery:
sections.preamble: Once the model reaction between benzenesulfonamide and chlorobenzene had finished, the mixture was cooled to room temperature. Subsequently, diethyl ether (10 mL) was introduced into the mixture and stirred for 10 minutes to aid in releasing the product from the catalyst. The catalyst was then allowed to settle, and the upper diethyl ether layer, containing the organic portion, was transferred into a separate round-bottom flask. This process was repeated at least three times to ensure complete extraction of the organic component, as confirmed by TLC analysis. Afterward, the reaction vessel containing the catalyst was thoroughly dried under high vacuum to obtain the powdered catalyst (Scheme S1), which was subsequently reused in successive reactions (Figure S2).

sections.heading: 7. Synthesis of tertiary sulfonamides by further reacting the C–N coupling product:
sections.preamble: The reaction was carried out using N-phenylbenzenesulfonamide (1) with either 1-chloro-4- methylbenzene or 1-bromo-4-methylbenzene as model substrates under the optimized conditions, providing the desired tertiary sulfonamide 73 in moderate yield.

sections.heading: 8. Reaction with TEMPO, BnOH, and BHT:
sections.preamble: The reaction was conducted in the presence of a few radical scavengers such as 2,2,6,6- tetramethylpiperidine-1-oxyl (TEMPO), benzyl alcohol (BnOH), and butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT), and a noteworthy amount of product, N-phenylbenzenesulfonamide (1) was still isolated, further supporting the conclusion that radical species are not involved in the reaction mechanism. These findings collectively indicate that the reaction proceeds through a non-radical pathway.

Figure S3b presents the X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analysis of copper in the reaction mixture. This scan confirms the presence of copper. The analysis revealed peaks at binding energies corresponding to Cu 2p₃/₂ and Cu 2p₁/₂, observed at approximately 931.6 eV and 951.9 eV, respectively. These findings indicate that Cu exists in the +1oxidation state within the active catalytic species.

records.heading: UV spectroscopy and Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) study:
records.text:
UV spectroscopy was analyzed from the reaction mixture between benzenesulfonamide and chlorobenzene in DMSO at standard conditions. Spectra of Fe(acac)₃, Fe(acac)₂, and CuI in DMSO were recorded to serve as references for comparison. The reaction mixture after 1 h and 15 h showed a peak resembling that of Fe(acac)2 at around 275 nm, which indicates the formation of iron (II) species in the reaction mixture (Figure S4a). Furthermore, the reaction mixture, both after 1 h and 15 h showed another peak similar to CuI at around 270 nm, which suggests the formation of Cu(I) species in the reaction mixture (Figure S4a). Additionally, after one hour of analysis, an additional peak at 305 nm appeared in the reaction mixture. This peak may arise from the formation of another iron intermediate generated during the catalytic cycle.
Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) analysis of the residual powder, collected after extracting the organic compounds, indicated the existence of both Fe(II) and Fe(III) species, along with Cu(I) (Figure S4b). This solid preserved its catalytic efficiency through four consecutive cycles, showing no appreciable decrease in activity (Figure S2).

sections.heading: 10. Plausible mechanistic pathway:
sections.preamble:
Based on mechanistic studies and prior literature reports, a plausible mechanistic pathway is proposed in Scheme S2. The proposed reaction mechanism proceeds through three elementary steps: (i) The aryl halide undergoes oxidative addition to the catalytically active copper(I) species A, generating intermediate B. The sulfonamide substrate or acetylacetonate (acac) might coordinate with the active catalytic species, potentially assisting in the oxidative addition process. (ii) transmetalation of intermediate B with an iron-amide species to yield intermediate C; and (iii) reductive elimination from intermediate C to produce the cross-coupling product and to regenerate the involved active copper(I) species A.
